speaker: mikikebrandstetter
text: Thank you, Ken. And that during this year, the prospect of what to do with the fireworks portion of the Lakewood Municipal Code got a lot of attention from the city council following all of this committee's efforts the previous year. And the council did take note of your recommendation to not make any changes to the code, but to be more aggressive with respect to an education program around it. However, the council began the year looking to say that we wanted to try to find a more robust library record of public input. And just about the time that we made that decision and scheduled a public hearing, we ended up with the meeting restrictions for COVID that made public hearings and such being virtual. And that has continued to do that. And ultimately, the council extended and rescheduled and extended and rescheduled and essentially had five periods of public comment in both virtually and through emails to do that with over 150 separate people sending in what they thought what the city should do about fireworks. In the end, the council, after distilling all of that, went through and did pass an ordinance that made some amendments to the municipal code. That was done recognizing that majority of the comments recommended or were looking for some change to the code, although there was not unanimity about what change should be made. There was support for completely banning fireworks and not having a period of time. There were support for a shorter or lesser period of time than existed in the code. And there was a smaller percentage of folks that looked to say, you leave it alone. I guess that I will tell you that in looking at that code, there was a theme about enforcement that was present in comments. And there was a theme about an understanding about what constituted legal fireworks already and what was already illegal. And that theme was that was generally misunderstood. Excuse me a second. So in the end, I've got a document, if Joanna could share, that would highlight just what changes were made in the code by the council. So the first change was in the definition section of where there was some rewording about the definition of consumer fireworks, which is a new term. And it was adopted because the state law changed the previous term that involved those fireworks that were legal to be sold and discharged by the public to redefine those as consumer fireworks when they did some revisions of the RCW. And the same with the term dangerous fireworks, which went through in that same way. It really is not those changes in definition are more in the titles of the terms rather than causing there to be any significant difference in how our code was. Further down under general provisions, and if we can move that down, Joanna, the general provisions section included the section where it talked about when fireworks were legal to be set off by members of the public. And it changed it from a three-day period in July to just a 12-hour period on the 4th of July. And it retained the two-hour period at the end of the year for fireworks at the New Year's. That it's important to note that this particular provision will be effective in 2022. In 2021, we will continue to have the previous three-day period because of state law requirements that require there to be at least 12 months' time between making a change in something like this and allowing it to become effective. So that then, if we could move on to there is another section of, and there's a section about exceptions, if we just go back up to exceptions. And the council did not discuss making some statement about exceptions, but then ultimately did not and just left the exceptions provisions to be exactly like it is in state law without any clarifying language to try to help educate what's legal and not illegal. Essentially, things that essentially are generally able to be used safely by children in terms of sparklers and caps are not covered by any of the restrictions around fireworks. And a lot of the explosive sort of things that go with funerals or commercial applications aren't subject to this. And lastly, the council made a change in the section regarding penalties, changing violations from being a misdemeanor with $1,000 fine and a 90-day jail term to gross disdemeanor, a $5,000 fine, and a 364-day potential jail term. Now, the reason that that was done was not that we were trying to take a look at folks who, members of the public, that were setting off fireworks outside the ordinance, but rather to align this with the state law. And these penalties are really intended to actually be primarily imposed for violations of the law and the code that relate to the sale of fireworks by vendors and others, that the far more likely is a section D under violation would be for most instances of where there would be an enforcement action by the city or on a citizen who was setting off personal fireworks, either because the fireworks themselves were illegal or it was outside the time, would be paragraph D, where we're really looking at a $75 fine, something that would be handled through an infraction process rather than a criminal process for gross disdemeanor. I guess that I will tell you that the council didn't, while it considered an outright ban on fireworks, decided not to go there, that the council also acknowledged the challenges with enforcement of this ordinance that the chief provided. And there was a general acknowledgment that the road to compliance is through an education program, as this committee had pointed out in its recommendation. And the chief's estimate that substantial compliance or change in the level of compliance would probably take as much as five years to be able to go through and do that. And also, the council, in looking at the budget that we adopted for 2021 and 2022, put some money in there to investigate and work on the viability of there becoming a significant public fireworks display put on by the city for the community. The challenge there is not cost, but actually finding a venue that would be both safe and yet visible and accessible to a significant amount of the public. And so we have provided some funding for the city manager, asking him to, by the end of the biennium, come up with a plan so that such a display can be programmed for beginning in 2023. That the council did discuss whether we should add any money to the police department budget for specifically funding an education program around fireworks, and ultimately decided, and I believe the chief at least concurred with the city manager that such a program, while needed, could be mounted with existing resources that existed within the police department budget as it was being approved for 2021 and 2022. So, Mr. Chair, I'm open to any questions about what we did and where we stand.

text: Good. Thank you, Mr. Chair. I'll start off first with trying to update a little bit more on the squad 21 that we talked about last time. A little bit more color for it, we're looking to do a 12-month evaluation. So that 12-month evaluation is up about the third week of January. So we're getting very close to have one-year data on the effectiveness on the call volume that that squad is able to pick up. Now, the squad 21, if you're not familiar with it, it's an old suburban. And what it's designed to do is to take some of the call volume away from our two busiest stations. And so our two busiest stations is 5,000 Silicon Boulevard, station 21, and station 20 off Pacific Highway. And the design for that squad 21, because it doesn't have a pump with it and it only has two firefighters on there, is the idea that it's going to respond to low acuity calls, falls, patient assist, beauty bark fires, things, or even like smoke alarm installations or problems, or people like service calls being locked out of their house, locked out of their car, something like that. So on average, it's been responding to anywhere from four to 10 calls during the day. And we only use it during our peak time, which is 8 o'clock in the morning to 8 o'clock at night. So it's not a 24-hour vehicle. It's just something that we use that we've identified during our busiest times. And also, during the day, over the last few years, we found it more and more difficult to keep crews being able to get their hands-on training. And so all of that training is done mostly at station 21 over there at 5,000 Silicon Boulevard because we have that concrete tower that we use. And by having that squad 21 available, we're able to use that and deploy them and keep crews in service so that they can get that hands-on training that they need. Any questions about the squad? We can certainly do, once the one-year evaluation period's over, we can have one of our operations chief put together a small presentation and do something if you want to put it on a work calendar for next year or something like that. But any questions?

speaker: alanhart

speaker: westpierce
text: Well, one of our biggest things is trying to look at our response times. And so with our medic units and our fire engines, certainly response times are going to be a little bit shorter. Or excuse me, they're going to be a little bit longer because the squad's going to be able to maneuver much quicker during a busy day or on an average call because they're so much smaller. We're also looking at how many miles, specifically our ladder truck, has been traveling. It's out of service a lot. It requires a lot of maintenance. And so by cutting down some of the call volume for that ladder truck, we're going to be able to save some life with the ladder truck, is the hope, and be able to keep those crews in service for the more major, serious calls, rescue calls, fire calls type thing. Because that engine currently is used on aid calls, ALS calls, which isn't a bad thing, but using your ladder truck all the time to run aid calls. And then you have a fire call, and that ladder truck is not able to free up for that fire. It just kind of takes that piece, or they're certainly delayed to that call. So we do have a gentleman that works with Fire Comm to pull that data. speaker: mikezaro
text: All right. Well, thank you all. Hope you all had a nice Thanksgiving. Just a couple of things to provide updates on, kind of an eclectic mix of updates. But first, as one thing that's kind of exciting and positive is, for the first time in quite a while, we have two new hires on the department that started on Monday, both entry-level officers. They start at the academy January 6. And it's been a long wait for them because they actually received their first conditional offer in the spring, right before COVID hit. And then COVID hit, and the whole world came to an end. So we had to put a hold on their hiring until just recently. So we were finally able to get them on board on Monday. And one, both, I think, are going to be outstanding additions to the department. One of the individuals is Kirsten Mundell. And it's fitting that she started the day after the 29th of November. You may recognize her last name. But her father, Kent Mundell, was a Pierce County deputy killed in 2009, a month after our four officers. So we have this tie with her already going in. So very special to be able to hire her. And I'm very proud to be able to hire her as well. Moving on, I mentioned the 29th. We had our annual food drive this year, food and blood drive. We weren't really expecting a whole lot. Just you never knew what to expect or know what to expect this year. But we ended up taking in about $14,000 and about 8,000 pounds of food. That's just on the day of the event here at the station. So all things considered, a very successful food drive that went to benefit the emergency food network. How did that compare with last year? It's less than last year. Last year, we had about $20,000 and about 20,000 pounds of food. But remember, last year was the 10th anniversary. So it garnered extra attention that this year didn't get. But even without the attention, we did pretty well this year. And speaking of the food drive, we have a couple other charity events that we hold every year. One is the shop with an officer where we partner with Walmart. And we're paired with families or officers are paired up with families in need and go and do some Christmas shopping with them, all paid for by the Lakewood Officers Charity. Just given the COVID circumstances and restrictions that we're under, we're evaluating how we can do that this year. We don't know if we will be able to. If we do, it won't be in the same format that we have done in years past, maybe a delivery of some sort. The other event that we have is called Holiday Meals, informally referred to as Moody Meals around here, because it was founded by Officer Ryan Moody. And what we do there is, again, we identify some families in need through the school district. And the Officers Charity buys a bunch of pre-made meals. Well, I shouldn't say pre-made, the ingredients for holiday meals. They provide a frozen turkey, stuff for mashed potatoes, and stuffing, and even vegetables, and a pie for dessert. Normally, the families come here and have a little pizza party and get their dinner before they go. And we deliver a few. But this year, because of the COVID restrictions, it's being held down at Tillicum Elementary in the gym. And there won't be a pizza party or anything else. It will just be a drive up and get their meal and go. So I'm happy that we're able to still provide that or hold that event, even though it's a little different format. And I think we'll be able to do something with the shop with an officer. But we're just not sure what that's going to look like yet. And again, just they're fantastic events. And I don't know if any of you've heard me talk about it before. But the shop with an officer in particular, I always remember my first year doing it and being paired with a little girl who, one of the things she wanted was a pillow for her sister so they didn't have to share anymore. So you hear stories like that. And it's just you know that the event is worthwhile. And it really does mean something to those families. And then two more items to update on, more, I guess, business matters for us. First is the Pierce County Forest Investigation Team. That's the countywide team that's being formed to investigate officer uses of deadly force. And as mandated by new state law, those investigations are conducted by independent teams made up of people other than or outside the involved agencies department. So here in Pierce County, about a year ago, all the agencies got together and decided that we're going to have a countywide team to meet that requirement. And I was, I guess, elected or asked to spearhead the effort. So the last year has been spent getting agreements together, getting the community representatives together that are needed for it, and then getting the applications from investigators from around the county. So the point we're at now is we have the interviews of the investigators. By law, the non-law enforcement representatives or the community representatives have to be involved in those interviews. Now, we have 59 applications from investigators from agencies around the county. And that includes the Washington State Patrol. Obviously, those interviews can all be done in one day. But our first day of interviews is going to be on Tuesday the 8th. And it will be with a small representative group of a larger group of community representatives. And we'll take all day. And there's a set block of questions that they'll be asking the investigators. So we'll see. We hope to get through 18 on that first day. And we'll probably have two or maybe even three more days of interviews after that before we get through that part of the process. So it has been a lot of work. I think we're making a lot of progress. And given what it was that we undertook, I think we're getting it done in about as quick of a timeline as you can hope for. The final little bit of update of business that we have here is we received notice of termination from the Nisqually Jail of our contract with them Friday before Thanksgiving. So we're working on other options. Their letter said that they were moving to scale back some of the jail services that they provide and focus more on the State Department of Corrections and their own internal tribal needs. So I've been in some communications with the jail chief or the police chief down there to work on a smooth transition out. But what we will likely do is be booking our misdemeanors back into the Pierce County Jail like we did years ago and have done for years. So operationally, I think the only change will be for our patrol officers not having to go to Nisqually. They'll go to Pierce County for our misdemeanors. Now, one of the drawbacks for that, for us operationally anyways, will be that Nisqually would take some people that, because of COVID restrictions, Pierce County wouldn't. So some of the people that were committing more the lower end nuisance crimes that Pierce County would not take because of COVID restrictions and Nisqually would, those folks were going to have to just release at the scene and write a report and maybe summons them later. So that will be a little bit tougher to deal with and work around sometimes. But it's nothing we can't work around or figure something out. So again, thanks. Just another gift from COVID, really, that we're going to have to deal with. But hopefully, in the spring, things start to loosen up a little bit. And things will, booking-wise anyways, get back to normal. What about the impact on your budget? So Nisqually was significantly cheaper than pretty much any other option out there. We looked at SCORE in South King County and Thurston County and Kitsap County just to see what some of their rates were like. And they were all significantly more than Nisqually. But Pierce County was not as much as those others. They were more than Nisqually, but not as much. So we are going to see it is going to be the amount that we budget for for the jail for 21 and 22 will likely be less than what we would need. However, we are also booking fewer people because of COVID. So without those bookings, it might at least for this coming year, for the next quarter or two, be a wash. But there will be a financial impact to that as well. And that, I know, was a very fast rundown and update on a few items we have going here. But I'd be happy to answer any questions that any of you have.
